summary: Defines a YANG module for the Dual-Stack Lite AFTR and B4 elements.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a settings form for the two parts of a system that carries old-style traffic over new-style networks.

questions: what is the aftr in ds-lite
subtitle: A YANG configuration schema for the two ends of a Dual-Stack Lite tunnel: the home-side B4 and the provider-side AFTR.

tldr.problem: Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) carries IPv4 traffic over an IPv6 network, but it had no standard, machine-readable way to configure and monitor its two elements, the B4 and the AFTR.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8513 defines the YANG module ietf-dslite. It adds DS-Lite settings to the standard Interfaces model and the NAT model, plus one statistic and one notification.
tldr.outcome: Operators can configure and watch B4 and AFTR devices through NETCONF or RESTCONF with a common data model. Writable nodes are sensitive, so access must be protected.

today: RFC 8513 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the YANG data model for DS-Lite. It builds on the NAT module in RFC 8512.

sections.title: What the Module Covers
sections.content:
RFC 8513 defines a data model for DS-Lite (described in RFC 6333) using the YANG data modeling language. It covers both elements of DS-Lite: the Address Family Transition Router (AFTR) and the Basic Bridging BroadBand element (B4).

It follows the YANG authoring guidelines of RFC 8407, uses the common types of RFC 6991, and adopts the Network Management Datastore Architecture from RFC 8342. Deployment questions for DS-Lite itself are left to RFC 6908.
sections.plainLanguage: DS-Lite has two machines that work as a team. This RFC writes down, in a standard way, all the knobs you can turn on each of them.

sections.title: The DS-Lite Architecture and the Two Elements
sections.content:
In the architecture drawn in the RFC, a host behind a home router reaches the Internet through an IPv4-in-IPv6 softwire across the provider's IPv6 core network. The B4 sits in the home router at one end. The AFTR sits at the provider end and combines a tunnel endpoint with a NAT.

The RFC states it simply: the AFTR is the combination of an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel and a NAPT function (see RFC 3022), while the B4 is just an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel. Because of that, the module is built as an augmentation of two existing models: the Interfaces module (RFC 8343) and the NAT module (RFC 8512).

A YANG feature statement, either aftr or b4, marks which data nodes apply to which element.
sections.plainLanguage: One machine at your house packs your old-style messages into a new-style envelope. The machine at the provider unpacks them and sends them on. The form has some boxes only for one machine and some for both.

sections.title: Interface Settings
sections.content:
The module augments each interface whose type is the new dslite identity (derived from the IANA tunnel interface type). The added settings are:

  • ipv6-address: the IPv6 address of the local tunnel endpoint, used to send and receive IPv4-in-IPv6 packets.
  • ipv4-address: an IPv4 address used for troubleshooting. The module says 192.0.0.1 is reserved for the AFTR and 192.0.0.0/29 for the B4. It can be used to report ICMP problems and appears in traceroute output.
  • aftr-ipv6-addr: the AFTR's IPv6 address, which a B4 uses to reach its AFTR. Only available with the b4 feature.
  • tunnel-mtu: the tunnel MTU. The module notes that the 40-byte IPv6 overhead should be accounted for in the network between the B4 and the AFTR.
  • v6-v4-dscp-preservation: whether the DSCP value is copied from the IPv4 header to the IPv6 Traffic Class field and back.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tunnel end gets a few boxes: its own address, the address of its partner, how big a package may be, and whether to keep the "priority sticker" on the package.

sections.title: AFTR Policies, Mapping Entries and Statistics
sections.content:
On the AFTR side, the module augments the NAT policy with four settings. max-softwires-per-subscriber (default 1) stops a misbehaving subscriber from building many softwires to grab more external ports or burn AFTR processing. state-migrate (default true) tells the AFTR to move existing state to a B4's new IPv6 address when it changes. b4-address-change-limit (default 1800 seconds, which is 30 minutes) rate-limits address changes, since frequent changes could be used for denial of service. mss-clamping holds an enable flag and an mss-value to rewrite the TCP Maximum Segment Size and avoid fragmentation.

Each NAPT44 mapping entry gains b4-ipv6-address (the B4's address and the time of its last change). This is needed because different subscribers may use overlapping IPv4 address space. When DSCP preservation is on, entries also record v6-dscp, internal-v4-dscp and external-v4-dscp. A statistic, active-softwires, counts the currently active softwires on an AFTR instance.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider-side machine has rules like "one tunnel per customer" and "do not let someone keep changing their address too fast." It also keeps a notebook of which customer each connection belongs to.

sections.title: Notifications and Examples
sections.content:
The module defines one notification, b4-address-change-limit-policy-violation. An AFTR generates it when a B4 unsuccessfully tries to change its IPv6 address in less time than the b4-address-change-limit. It carries the NAT instance id, the policy id and the offending B4 address, and notifications are themselves rate-limited.

Appendix A shows a B4 named myB4 with address 2001:db8:0:1::1, configured with the AFTR address 2001:db8:0:2::1 and told to preserve DSCP. Appendix B shows an AFTR at 2001:db8:0:2::1 with the troubleshooting IPv4 address 192.0.0.1. Access control lists, QoS policies and Port Control Protocol are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone keeps changing their address too quickly, the provider machine rings a bell to tell the people in charge. The RFC also gives sample filled-in forms.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH and TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model can restrict which users may reach which data. All writable nodes are considered sensitive, because unprotected writes can hurt network operations.

The RFC lists attacks an intruder could attempt: pointing aftr-ipv6-addr at an illegitimate AFTR to intercept all of a B4's traffic (a severe privacy problem), setting a low tunnel-mtu to cause more fragments, setting max-softwire-per-subscriber very high, setting state-migrate to false, setting b4-address-change-limit very low, and turning off v6-v4-dscp-preservation.
sections.plainLanguage: Because these settings control where people's traffic goes, only trusted people should be allowed to change them. Otherwise someone could send your mail through a stranger's machine.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-dslite in the IETF XML Registry. It also registered the YANG module ietf-dslite with prefix dslite in the YANG Module Names registry, referencing RFC 8513. The module revision is dated 2019-01-10.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name list now includes this form, so nobody else can use the same name.
